Hormuz: a third US aircraft carrier arrives and Iran announces a fourth tanker on fire, but Brent falls 3.6%

On Monday, November 16, the US military confirmed the arrival of the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt in the Middle East, the third in the region [3][4]. The same day, the Iranian navy claimed that a fourth tanker had caught fire after hitting a mine near Hormuz [1][2]. Yet a barrel of Brent lost 3.6%, to $92.44 [6].
The Theodore Roosevelt entered the area of US Central Command on Sunday, November 15; a US official confirmed it on Monday [3][4][5].

It joins the carriers George H.W. Bush and George Washington, which are maintaining a naval blockade of Iranian ships; it was originally meant to replace the George Washington, which is staying in place for now [4][5].

Iran's regular navy says a tanker caught fire in the last 24 hours in a restricted zone east of the strait, without giving its name, flag, cargo or the condition of the crew; this has not been independently verified [1][2].
According to state television IRIB, the ship had switched off its navigation systems and suffered heavy damage [2].

Separately, the British maritime agency UKMTO reports an engine-room fire on a tanker about 7 nautical miles north of Khasab, in Oman, with the crew safe, but cannot say whether it is the same ship [2].
On Sunday, Iran also targeted a US helicopter base in Bahrain, its first strike against a Gulf country in weeks [4].
Brent closed Monday down $3.40, at $92.44: the International Energy Agency expects supply of 105 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, 1.7 million more than demand [6][7].
Key takeaway: on the ground, tension is rising, but markets are betting on more plentiful oil. Iranian announcements of attacks no longer send prices soaring [6][7].

Washington is reinforcing its blockade with thousands of extra troops, while Donald Trump alternates between threats of new strikes and the idea that the war is “militarily almost over” [4]. The unpopularity of this conflict weighed on the heavy Republican defeat in the midterm elections [4].

On the oil side, Middle East exports are picking up again and China is refining less: 2% less in October than in September, and 8.1% less than a year ago [7]. The bank Goldman Sachs sees Brent averaging $88 next year, then $78 at the end of 2027 [6].
But the risk remains real: BMI analysts consider the recovery in OPEC+ exports “fragile”, and Goldman Sachs points out that attacks on ships can push prices back up in the short term [6].

The price of a barrel quickly shows up in the price of a full tank and of heating oil. If it keeps falling, you could feel it at the pump within a few weeks. But a single confirmed sunken ship, or an escalation involving the US carriers, can reverse the trend overnight.

Wall Street: the Nasdaq falls 2.5% and enters a correction as Washington shuts the door on AI chips rented remotely by China

On Monday, November 16, the Nasdaq lost 2.49%, the S&P 500 1.92% and the Dow 1.41%. The chipmakers' index plunged more than 5% after a new US rule against China's remote access to AI chips, on the eve of results from Nvidia, which still has no CEO [1][2][5][13].

At the close, the S&P 500 fell to 7,416.59 points (−1.92%), the Nasdaq to 24,509.76 points (−2.49%) and the Dow Jones to 51,608.17 points (−1.41%), according to Reuters' wrap-up [1][9]. It was a third straight decline for the S&P 500 [1].
The Nasdaq is now more than 10% below its October 6 record: this is what financiers call a “correction” [2][9].

Chipmakers were hit hardest [3]: the Philadelphia SOX index lost 5.28%, to 9,610.65 points. Nvidia ended at $156.14 (−4.12%) and AMD gave up more than 5% [2][15]. Tech stocks lost about $960 billion in value [12].

The same day, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the Commerce Department office in charge of exports, published an interim rule: a license is now required to send advanced AI chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, considered at risk of “diversion” to China [5][6].

The rule also targets data centers outside China that rent a lot of computing power to Chinese companies: according to the BIS, the restrictions must not be able to be “circumvented” through such remote rentals [7][8].

Nvidia still has no CEO: Jensen Huang resigned on November 11, and chief financial officer Colette Kress is acting as interim [10]. According to the Washington Post, his departure follows the revelation of an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China; the company has given no explanation [10][11].
Key takeaway: the US stock market is having doubts about artificial intelligence, the engine that has carried it for months, and politics is getting involved [4][9].

The new rule hits the heart of Nvidia's and AMD's market directly. Chinese companies could rent chips installed elsewhere without importing them: Washington is closing this loophole, at the risk of slowing sales [6][7]. For CBS News and Al Jazeera, the measure comes right after the scandal that brought down Jensen Huang [8][9].

Interest rates are also weighing. The US 10-year yield was hovering around 5.14% on Monday morning [14]. When a safe investment pays that much, stocks that mainly promise future profits are less attractive [4][14].

Before the open, Nvidia was already coming off its longest streak of weekly declines since October 2012 [13]. For an analyst quoted by Reuters, Nvidia's results and the success of Anthropic's stock market listing will be “the barometer” of whether the correction continues [13].

If you have a “World” or “S&P 500” ETF in your PEA or life insurance policy, you have probably seen its value drop: the US tech giants weigh heavily in them. A 10% correction is nothing exceptional, and Nvidia's results could move prices in either direction.

Xi-Trump-Putin summit: Beijing promises a “historic” meeting on “world peace”, Trump wants to talk about Ukraine despite his advisers

On Monday, November 16, China confirmed that Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin will meet on Thursday the 19th in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC summit, to talk about “world peace” [1]. Trump flew off to Asia [2][3]. On Tuesday the 17th, the APEC CEO summit opens in the city [6][7].
According to Chinese spokeswoman Mao Ning, the three leaders will have “in-depth exchanges” on peace and “strategic stability” between major powers, a meeting of “revolutionary significance” [1].
Washington mainly wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals and the war in Iran; according to US officials, Ukraine was not on the agenda [4][1].

Trump nevertheless said he would talk about the war in Ukraine, and that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un “could come” to Shenzhen, “it's up to Xi” [3]. Elon Musk is accompanying him to Shenzhen, amid turmoil for Nvidia [9].
Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov says a one-on-one Trump-Putin meeting is being prepared [1].
According to the Globe and Mail, the three sides had still not set the agenda, or even the format, of the meeting as of this weekend [5].

The APEC CEO summit, organized by the Chinese trade promotion agency, is being held on November 17 and 18, with an opening speech by Xi [7]; Russian agency TASS announces more than 2,000 participants and a first final text in the form of a “Shenzhen Initiative” [6].
The China-US trade truce, extended by two months until January 10, should also be discussed; analysts expect a further extension [10][8].
Key takeaway: this is the first three-way meeting of the leaders of the three biggest military powers, but each is coming with a different goal [1][4].

Trump wants a deal on nuclear weapons; Beijing talks more about “peace” and “stability”; Putin hopes for a settlement of the war in Ukraine favorable to Moscow, a subject Xi and Trump are expected to avoid, according to observers [1].

Europeans, absent from APEC, fear that the three men will divide the world into “spheres of influence”; some are already comparing the meeting to the one at Yalta, in Crimea, in February 1945 [5]. Ukraine's foreign minister believes it “will only encourage Putin to continue this war” [1].

On the other hand, UN Secretary-General António Guterres believes that if the three “really commit” to disarmament, it would be “a great achievement for the world” [1]. For Trump, weakened by the loss of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, the trip is also a chance to change the subject [3].

What is said on Thursday in Shenzhen can weigh on the war in Ukraine, on Europe's doorstep, and on tariffs between China and the United States. If the trade truce holds, prices of electronics or of the rare metals used in your phone stay more stable. If it breaks, everything gets more complicated.

Civil servants: eight unions united in a strike this Tuesday to unfreeze the pay index point, 17 stations closed in Paris and high schools under watch

This Tuesday, November 17, civil servants, teachers, rail workers, university and high school students are called to strike and demonstrate across France. The unions are demanding that the index point, which is used to calculate public employees' salaries, be unfrozen. The Lecornu government refuses and is offering a month of talks on low wages [1][3][4].
The call was launched by six public-sector unions (CGT, UNSA, FSU, Solidaires, CFE-CGC and FAFP), then joined by Force ouvrière and by the CFDT's public-sector branch [1][4].

The CFDT switched sides after the November 13 meeting at Matignon, from which the union alliance came out “fired up”: Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu only offered a month of talks on five topics, including low wages [2][4].
According to CGT État, the government once again refused any increase in the index point; the unions are demanding an immediate raise, indexation to inflation and an overhaul of pay scales [3].
The Education Ministry expects 3.73% of staff to strike in public schools; during the previous day of action, nearly 10% of civil servants had stopped work [1].

At SNCF, CGT-Cheminots, SUD-Rail and CFDT-Cheminots are calling a strike; TGV Inoui trains should run normally, but suburban lines D, J, N and R are disrupted in the Île-de-France region [5]. Ouest-France reports a “limited impact” on transport and the CGT counts nearly 179 events across the country [6].
In Paris, 17 metro and RER stations are closed from 11 a.m. at the request of the police prefecture [7].

The prefecture is banning undeclared gatherings within 100 meters of ten high schools and five university sites until November 27; in Rennes, the administrative court ordered classes to resume at two blockaded high schools, Bréquigny and Descartes [5].
Key takeaway: this is the broadest union front since the start of the social crisis, with all eight public-sector organizations in the same strike [3][4].
The index point is the common basis for the salaries of millions of public employees: when it is frozen, their pay stagnates while prices rise. That is why the unions want it to track inflation [3].

For the government, the equation is budgetary: every across-the-board increase is expensive, just as it is looking for savings in the 2027 budget. It prefers to target the lowest wages, a response that employee representatives consider largely insufficient [2][4].

The day is also a test. If turnout stays modest, as the Education Ministry's forecast suggests, Matignon will be able to hold its line; if it exceeds the previous one, pressure will build during the month of talks [1][4].

If you take the suburban train in Île-de-France or the metro in central Paris, have a plan B this Tuesday. If you are a high school or university student, classes may be cancelled, and around some Paris schools undeclared gatherings are banned until November 27.

Ukraine: for the first time, Europe sits at the table with Kyiv and Washington, with a meeting Thursday in Berlin, while a Crimean bridge is struck

On Monday, November 16, Volodymyr Zelensky announced online talks between Ukrainian, American and European negotiators, a first for Europe [1][2]. Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, are due to meet Ukrainians and Europeans on Thursday the 19th in Berlin [4]. Overnight, Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge [5][6].

On the US side, Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner and General Alex Grynkewich, NATO's military commander, took part; on the European side, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy, Poland, NATO and the EU institutions [1][3].
“The discussion was difficult, but there is a result: we will meet in Berlin within the framework of the Coalition of the Willing,” Zelensky said [2].
Jared Kushner describes three “pillars”: strong security guarantees, a path to EU membership and a postwar prosperity plan prepared with the Europeans and the World Bank [4].
He acknowledges that “significant challenges remain” and that a final deal will have to be accepted by Russia and Ukraine [4].
Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov says Moscow has not agreed to the presence of the Europeans at the next round [3].
Russia says it intercepted 1,336 Ukrainian drones overnight from Sunday to Monday, a record since 2022; according to the mayor of Moscow, 600 were aimed at the capital [5][6].
Traffic on the Crimean Bridge was halted around 2:22 a.m. Moscow time; a single lane reopened about 17 hours later [5][1].
Key takeaway: the Europeans, long kept out of talks between Americans, Russians and Ukrainians, are finally getting a seat, but Moscow has not approved it [1][3].

Zelensky specifies that Europe was represented “in full” by those who will represent it facing the Russians [3]. These talks follow the meetings in Abu Dhabi between Americans, Russians and Ukrainians [3].

On the ground, Kyiv is striking deep inside Russia. The Crimean Bridge, which links the annexed peninsula to Russia, is vital for supplying the Russian army; the Kremlin speaks of minor damage [5][1].
Zelensky also warned that Kyiv had intelligence about major Russian strikes planned for Monday evening, overnight and Tuesday [1].

Peace in Ukraine is also at stake for France, which is at the table: security guarantees, financial aid, reconstruction. An end to the war would ease pressure on energy and on European military budgets, and therefore on the taxes and prices you pay.

2027 budget: if Lecornu uses ordinances, “there will be a no-confidence vote”, the PS warns, three days before the Senate debate

On Monday, November 16, Socialist Party (PS) first secretary Olivier Faure promised to vote for a no-confidence motion if Sébastien Lecornu has the 2027 budget adopted by ordinance, a procedure never used under the Fifth Republic. The bill, which targets a deficit of 5% of GDP with a 54 billion euro effort, reaches the Senate on November 20 [2][3][4][7].

On BFMTV-RMC, Olivier Faure said he did not know what the Prime Minister is planning, but insisted that if he uses ordinances, a no-confidence vote is certain; the “suspense” is “nonexistent”, he added [1][2][3].
Article 47 of the Constitution allows the government to implement its budget by ordinance if Parliament has not ruled within 70 days; the deadline runs until midnight on December 17 [4].
This route does not open if Parliament rejects the bill. The other option, Article 49.3, also exposes the government to a no-confidence vote which, if passed, would mean the budget is rejected [4].
On November 4, MPs unanimously rejected the “revenue” part of the bill: the Senate therefore receives the government's original text, without the National Assembly having debated spending [5].

The Senate finance committee, with general rapporteur Christine Lavarde, wants to improve the balance by about 0.2 point of GDP, or nearly 6 billion euros, and proposes 400 million euros more for universities [8][9].

The government expects a deficit of 5% of GDP in 2027, after 5.4% in 2026, thanks to an effort of 54 billion euros; without savings, the deficit would approach 6.5%, according to Sébastien Lecornu [6].
Public debt would rise from 119.3% to 121.7% of GDP, a record [7], and interest costs from 79.2 billion euros in 2026 to 91.2 billion in 2027 [10].
Key takeaway: without a majority in the National Assembly, the government has only risky ways out, and the PS has just closed off the ordinance route [2][4].
The timetable is tight. Senators debate in plenary from November 20, then a joint committee will try to reconcile MPs and senators; the Senate plans its final votes in early December [9][11].

A budget ordinance would be a historic first: it would allow the budget to be implemented without a vote, but would expose the government to a no-confidence motion. According to Public Sénat, the government could then fall while leaving the budget in force, a point that legal experts are still debating [4].

This is not Faure's first threat: as early as September, he promised a no-confidence vote if nothing changed on the limited increase in health spending, the de-indexation of pensions and the freeze of civil servants' index point [12].

This budget decides your taxes, your grandparents' pensions and your university's resources. If it is not passed in time, the state can operate under a special law, but new measures remain blocked. And every extra billion in interest on the debt is one billion less for schools or health.

Russia: the EU sanctions 140 refineries, banks and backers of the shadow fleet, and announces a 22nd package targeting visas and athletes

On Monday, November 16 in Brussels, EU foreign ministers approved 140 new listings on the sanctions list against Russia: refineries, banks, e-commerce sites and companies in the Gulf and East Asia that help the shadow fleet. Kaja Kallas promises a 22nd package “in the coming days” [1][2].

The 140 listings target Russian refineries and banks, e-commerce players, as well as companies in the Gulf and East Asia that support the “shadow fleet”, the tankers that carry Russian oil while getting around sanctions [1].
It is also the largest set of sanctions to date against those responsible for Russian cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns targeting the EU, according to EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas [1].
Announced before the meeting, these measures had not yet been quantified: the EU finally settled on 140 [1][4].
The 22nd sanctions package is due to be presented in the coming days, to increase pressure on Moscow in the absence of progress toward a ceasefire in Ukraine [1][2].

It could tighten the issuing of visas to Russians and ban Russian athletes from competitions held in the EU; Kaja Kallas acknowledges that some member states still have questions about implementation [1][3].
Three days earlier, on November 13, troops from the European operation Irini had inspected the tanker MV Midag in the Mediterranean and confirmed that it was sailing under a false flag [4][5].
Key takeaway: the EU is now striking beyond Russia, targeting the countries and companies that help it sell its oil [1].

The shadow fleet is the lifeblood of the war: these ships, often under false flags, allow Moscow to export its oil despite the price cap and to finance its army. The inspection of the MV Midag was carried out under Article 110 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea [4][5].

Sanctions are piling up: the 20th package, adopted on April 23 after Hungary lifted its veto, had added 120 individuals and entities and banned transactions with Russian cryptocurrency platforms [7]; the 21st, in July, targeted energy, financial services and crypto [6].
The timing is diplomatic: Europeans want to carry weight while peace negotiations are largely being conducted without them. Kaja Kallas repeats that the priority must be a ceasefire [2].

Less Russian oil sold on the sly means less money for the war in Ukraine, but also a slightly tighter oil market, which can show up at the pump. And if you follow sports, a ban on Russian athletes in competitions held in the EU would change the face of several championships.

Fed: Kevin Warsh prepares three scenarios for AI, including a wave of unemployment and a crash, as the US 10-year yield stays above 5%

On Monday, November 16 in San Francisco, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh presented three scenarios for artificial intelligence: a shared boom, a boom that leaves workers behind, or a failure that sends the stock market tumbling. Nothing on rates, while the US 10-year yield was hovering around 5.13% [1][2][4].
Warsh opened a Fed conference on productivity and employment, saying that AI will matter for the economy as well as for monetary policy [1][2].
First scenario: AI triggers a productivity boom whose gains benefit both companies and workers [1][3].
Second scenario: growth accelerates, but AI replaces workers and unemployment rises [1][3].
Third scenario: the profits expected from huge investments in AI do not materialize, which would drag down the stock market and growth [1][3].
“These are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts,” Warsh said, adding that the Fed's role was “neither to champion nor to fight” AI [1].
He described US productivity as “fairly solid” in recent quarters, without yet seeing a clear and lasting increase [3].
His prepared remarks said nothing about rates, inflation or the December meeting [2][4].
Key takeaway: the world's most powerful central bank is taking seriously the possibility that the AI race ends badly, just as markets are doubting its promises [1][4].
On Monday, AI-related stocks were sold off again ahead of Nvidia's results, due this week: the session was marked by a new decline in big tech stocks on Wall Street [4][5][6].

On rates, the yield on 10-year US government bonds was hovering around 5.13%, after peaking at 5.15% on November 13, as investors bet on a Fed rate hike in December [2]. A high 10-year yield makes all credit more expensive (mortgages, business loans) and weighs on growth stocks, whose future profits are worth less when money costs more [6].

Several Fed officials are pushing in this direction: Governor Christopher Waller said on November 10 that he leaned toward a quarter-point hike and that a half point “should be considered” if core inflation stayed around 0.3% per month, which it was in October [7]. At the Dallas Fed, Lorie Logan is calling for at least two more hikes [8]. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said this weekend that inflation was now the main criterion [5].

When US rates rise, European rates tend to follow: mortgages and student loans can become more expensive in France. And if you have some savings invested in stocks (life insurance, PEA, World ETF), a large part depends on the US AI giants: the scenario of AI failing, considered by the Fed itself, concerns you directly.

Migrants: five EU countries want to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda from 2027, a “historic paradigm shift” for Vienna

On Monday, November 16 in Vienna, Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands presented, together with Rwanda, a plan for a “return hub” for migrants whose asylum claims have been rejected, the first outside the European Union. A pilot phase of about a hundred people is being considered, with an opening in 2027 [1][2][3].

Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker hailed a “historic paradigm shift”: people with no right to stay will be sent to a third country such as Rwanda if their return to their country of origin is impossible [4][5].
According to diplomatic sources, each country would initially send around twenty people, probably adult men arrested at the border, making it a kind of pilot project of about 100 people [1][2].

Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta promises “a second chance”: those received will be able to return home voluntarily, integrate in Rwanda or leave for a country where they have the right to live [4]. Kigali prefers to speak of “reception centers” and could offer vocational training there [1].
Asked about Rwanda's human rights record, Vincent Biruta dismissed the criticism as a “cliché” [4].

Human Rights Watch points to a “well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment”, and Kigali's support for an armed group in DR Congo; the UNHCR demands respect for international law [4].
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt insists the project will respect human rights as well as European and German law [4]. About a hundred demonstrators protested in Vienna [1].
Key takeaway: Europe is moving from idea to practice on deporting migrants to a third country with which they have no connection [2][5].

It is a European reform adopted earlier in 2026 that makes this possible: it expands detention powers and authorizes these “return hubs” [2][4]. The European Commission says it is “closely following” the five countries' preparatory work [4].

The project nevertheless divides the Twenty-Seven. Emmanuel Macron said these centers are “neither effective” nor in line with the Union's values [1], and NGOs challenge the idea of sending people to a country they do not know [5].
For the five governments, the stakes are also political: showing that they are acting on deportations, one of the issues fueling the rise of anti-immigration parties in Europe [3][5].

France is not part of the project, but European asylum rules apply here too. If the model works, pressure will grow for Paris to join; if it is struck down by the courts, it will serve as a warning. Either way, it is a debate that will come back in the 2027 presidential election.

Canada: in Shenzhen, Carney and Xi Jinping showcase “more stable” relations while negotiations with Trump stall

The two leaders praise cooperation relaunched since January; Ottawa announces new flights, a business leaders' forum and $15 million in cultural contracts [1][3][4].

Sweden: the Centre Party drops Kristersson for the left, but forming a government stumbles over the Left Party's demands

Two months after the general election, Sweden still has no government. On Sunday, November 15, the Centre Party chose to negotiate with Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson rather than with outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, who reports to the Speaker of Parliament this Tuesday. The Left Party is still demanding ministerial posts [1][2][3].
The Centre Party preferred Magdalena Andersson's offer to that of Ulf Kristersson, who heads a caretaker government: a heavy blow to his plan for a center-right coalition [3][4].

According to Swedish media cited by Xinhua, Ulf Kristersson now has little chance of forming a government; he is due to take stock on Tuesday, November 17 with the Speaker of Parliament, Andreas Norlén [3][6].
The government Magdalena Andersson wants, with the Centre Party and the Greens, would have only 146 seats and would need the Left Party's 30 MPs to survive a confidence vote [6].
The Left Party maintains its demand for ministerial posts; Ida Gabrielsson acknowledges that “no party can get all its demands” and is calling for a vote in Parliament on Kristersson's candidacy [1].
The Centre Party repeats that it will not support a government that includes Left Party ministers [2].
On November 3, Parliament had already rejected Centre Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist as Prime Minister: only her party's 25 MPs had voted for her [5].
Key takeaway: the small Centre Party is deciding Sweden's next government, but it refuses to govern with the ally the left needs [2][6].
In the September 13 election, the center-left bloc won 176 seats against 173 for Kristersson's right; the Social Democrats came first with 28% of the vote, and the Centre Party got only 7% [7].

The Speaker of Parliament must consult party leaders before deciding on a vote on Kristersson; Magdalena Andersson should then get a week, which can be extended, to negotiate [2]. Talks between the Social Democrats, the Centre Party, the Left Party and the Greens were due to resume as early as Monday [2].

The election result is not enough: although it has a majority on paper, this bloc remains divided over the role of the Left Party, which raises the risk of another failed vote in Parliament [1][2][5].

Sweden carries weight in European decisions, from aid to Ukraine to the EU budget. As long as Stockholm only has a caretaker government, its commitments remain limited. And this deadlock shows what happens when no side has a majority, a scenario France knows well.

“I did my best”: ten years after his candidacy, Macron admits “mistakes”, the left-wing opposition replies “grim anniversary”

On Monday, November 16, ten years to the day after announcing his first candidacy in Bobigny, Emmanuel Macron published a long text on X taking stock. Six months before the end of his second term, the president admits “sometimes mistakes” but insists he acted “in the higher interest of the country” [1][2][4].
The message was published on X on Monday, without a speech or official staging, to mark the anniversary of the announcement of his candidacy on November 16, 2016 [2][3].
That announcement had taken place at an apprenticeship center in Bobigny, in Seine-Saint-Denis, a few months after he left François Hollande's government [2].
“There were sometimes mistakes, but every day we worked hard,” writes the head of state, who says he did his best [1][5].
He says he acted in the higher interest of the country, including toward those who did not vote for him, and credits the work done to “many remarkable women and men” [2][4].
The text sets out no outlook for after 2027 [3]; the Constitution bars him from a third consecutive term [1].
The head of the LFI group in the National Assembly, Mathilde Panot, replied on X, denouncing a “grim anniversary”, marked in her view by social destruction and the stifling of democracy [1][3].
The Communist presidential candidate, Fabien Roussel, replied with a simple “Goodbye” and called this mea culpa “shameful” [1][3].
Key takeaway: Macron is entering the home stretch of his presidency and is starting to write the story of his ten years himself, before the presidential campaign overshadows it [1][3].

The timing is not insignificant. The same day, public-sector unions were preparing a new day of strikes over pay, and the Socialist Party was threatening to bring down Sébastien Lecornu's government over the 2027 budget [6][7].

Admitting mistakes without naming them allows him to respond to his unpopularity without reopening contentious issues. That is precisely what his left-wing opponents criticize him for, as they believe the social record speaks for itself [1][3].
For his camp, the issue is succession: a president who cannot run again carries less weight with the majority and with the candidates who want to take over [1][3].

The 2027 presidential election will be fought partly on the record of these ten years: purchasing power, public services, pensions. Candidates will either claim it or distance themselves from it. If you are voting for the first time in the spring, now is the time to look at what has changed for you since 2017, beyond the slogans.

Mexico: Trump goes on the attack again and threatens more tariffs, while Sheinbaum insists “there are no more caravans” heading to the United States

On November 16, Donald Trump again threatened Mexico with heavy tariffs if Claudia Sheinbaum does not stop the migrant caravans heading north. The Mexican president repeats that no caravan has reached the US border since January 2025, and that the latest one has dispersed [1][2][3][4].

New on November 16: Trump is insisting, five days after promising to “immediately double” tariffs on Mexican products if the caravans are not stopped; however, he has not announced any concrete measure [1][2][3].

The caravan in question, which left Tapachula, in the state of Chiapas on the border with Guatemala, on November 10, numbered about 1,500 people according to a local government source, mostly Central Americans [1][2][3].
On November 12, Sheinbaum said that since Trump's return to power, no caravan had reached the northern border, and that only two groups had been spotted in the south of the country [5][6].
On November 14, she said there were “no more caravans” on the way: a group of 500 to 600 people formed in Arriaga (Chiapas) now has fewer than 100 members, most having returned home [4][7].
A new caravan was nevertheless due to leave Honduras, despite the blockade put in place by Mexico [1][2].
US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin promised on X to use “all resources” to protect the borders [1][2].
Key takeaway: for Trump, tariffs have become a weapon to win concessions on issues that have nothing to do with trade, such as immigration [3][5].

For Mexico, the stakes are huge: the United States is by far its biggest customer, and doubling tariffs would hit its export-oriented factories hard. Sheinbaum is therefore betting on de-escalation, showing with figures that the caravans disperse before reaching the north of the country [4][5][6].

The scenario is not new: back in late 2024, Trump had threatened Mexico with tariffs over the caravans, then claimed that she had agreed to stop migration; Sheinbaum had disputed this version, saying that Mexico wanted to “build bridges” and not close its borders [8].

A trade war between the United States and Mexico does not affect you directly, but many cars and parts sold in the United States are assembled in Mexico, including by European groups such as Renault-Nissan, Stellantis or Volkswagen. Every Trump threat weakens their factories and can affect their results, and therefore jobs and prices.

news.2026-11-17-venezuela-greve-national: Venezuela: hospitals, schools and universities on national strike to demand a $960 year-end bonus

On Monday, November 16, Venezuelan health, education and university unions held a 12-hour national strike, the fourth this year. They want year-end bonuses calculated on $240 per month, or $960 per worker. In health care, they claim 80% of staff went on strike [1][2][3].
The strike lasted from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. in several states of the country; it had been decided on November 5 at an inter-union assembly at the Central University of Venezuela (UCV), in Caracas [1][4].
Central demand: that the four months of year-end bonuses (“aguinaldos”) be calculated on a “comprehensive” monthly income of $240, which would come to $960 per worker [1][3].

The unions are also demanding a timetable for folding the bonuses into base pay, and an end to the “Sistema Patria”, the public platform through which the state currently pays part of salaries [1][4].

According to the director of the NGO Monitor Salud, 80% of health workers joined the strike, notably at the Periférico de Catia hospital in Caracas; a minimum service was maintained in emergency rooms [2].
This figure comes from unions and NGOs: no independent or government estimate has been published [2].
According to university leaders, this is the fourth national work stoppage since January [1].

Key takeaway: Venezuela has been trying to get back on its feet since the fall of Nicolás Maduro, but public employees feel they are not benefiting from this recovery, and social protest is getting organized [5][6].

The same day, the central bank set the official rate at 914.02 bolivars to the dollar [7]. When the national currency loses value, salaries paid in bolivars melt away: that is why the unions put their demands in dollars [1][7].

Delcy Rodríguez's government wants to show that the country is restarting: state oil company PDVSA is aiming for 3 million barrels per day within ten years, and the authorities on Monday began paying a “comprehensive income” to public-sector retirees [5]. But the mayors of Greater Caracas are calling for a state of emergency over power and water cuts [5].

The country is also trying to reconnect with international lenders: on November 13, the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) approved its first roadmap for Venezuela since it stopped lending in May 2018. But no new loans are possible until Caracas repays it $2.3bn in arrears [6].

Venezuela has the world's largest oil reserves: its social stability matters for global crude supply, and therefore indirectly for the price of filling your tank. And this strike is a reminder of a simple rule: when inflation eats away at a currency, it is first the employees paid in local currency, such as teachers and health workers, who suffer.
